card.hook: Most old town streets squeeze you into a corner, but Altmarkt does the opposite and gives you room to step back. That's rare in a historic centre, so enjoy it.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 65 m west of the subject, and face east. The whole square opens out in front of you, with its edges leading your eye in.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole square in, then switch to 1x for a more natural look. Try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out details on the far side.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep the building edges straight, and if the sky is bright, tap the middle of the scene and slide it a little darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Early morning usually has fewer people, so go then if you want an emptier square. Evening light can be pleasant, and night mode helps once it gets dark.
card.selfie_here: Climb the Kreuzkirche tower to the viewing platform at about 54 m, at the southeast corner of the Altmarkt. Use the front camera at 0.5x and turn so the square spreads out behind your shoulder.
card.challenge: Crouch a little lower, put a line of paving in the bottom third, and wait for someone to stroll through the frame. Congratulations, you just added scale and a bit of drama.
card.good_to_know: Altmarkt is the old market square in the heart of Dresden's Altstadt, in the Innere Altstadt. Think of it as a place to soak up the old town's atmosphere rather than a single landmark. It can get busy or have temporary structures, so be ready to move around.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 65 m west of the subject, and face east. The whole square opens out in front of you, with its edges leading your eye in.

selfie_spots.why: The platform looks down over the square and the old town, so a selfie taken there can show the Altmarkt spread out behind you.

card.hook: Plot twist: this Baroque beauty looks like it has stood untouched for centuries, but it was only reconsecrated in 2005. Its bell-shaped dome still owns the Dresden skyline.
card.stand_here: Head for Neumarkt square and stand at the phone icon on the map, about 90 m south-west of the church. Face north-east and the whole church is in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the church and its dome in together. Try zoom 0.5x for more of the square and the buildings around it, or zoom 2x-5x (if your phone has it) to home in on the dome and stonework.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, line the centre of the dome up with a vertical line, and hold the phone level so the walls don't lean.
card.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light brings out the colour of the stone, and the square is usually quieter early in the day. After dark, try night mode and rest your elbows on something steady.
card.selfie_here: Stand at the Martin Luther statue on Neumarkt, right in front of the church, so the facade and dome are behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a little low and switch to 0.5x if your phone offers it, so the dome fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand in the middle of Neumarkt facing the church while you stand in front of it, so the whole church fits behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the church, photos for personal use are generally fine, but no flash. Keep quiet and flash-free during services and choir performances, and check the official site for visiting arrangements and any dress or entry rules.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the dome sits dead straight on a gridline and a stranger walks past the front. Bonus points if they have no idea they're your scale model.
card.good_to_know: This is the third church on this site, built between 1726 and 1743 to a design by city architect George Bähr. It was destroyed in the bombing of February 1945, and its ruins stood for nearly half a century as a war memorial. The original dome, the 'Stone Bell', was about 67 metres high. Right next to it: Neumarkt.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for Neumarkt square and stand at the phone icon on the map, about 90 m south-west of the church. Face north-east and the whole church is in front of you.

card.hook: Turn around almost anywhere at the Zwinger and something carved is looking back at you: a statue, a vase, a balustrade showing off. It's a very photogenic place, so don't rush it.
card.stand_here: Stand about 75 m north-west of the Zwinger, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. You'll be looking across the whole complex instead of up at one wall.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the long galleries and pavilions into one frame. Switch to 1x for a single building, then 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the statues, vases and the Kronentor.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest stone area, then slide the brightness down a touch so the pale facades keep their carved detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer, warmer light on the stonework and fewer people in your shot. On a dull day the carved detail still looks great.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Kronentor (Crown Gate), the Zwinger's main entrance, and use the front camera at 0.5x with the gate over your shoulder. One guide suggests posing as if you're wearing the gate's crown, and you can shoot it from both sides.
card.ask_someone: Hand your phone to someone on Theaterplatz as you approach the Zwinger with the Semper Opera House on your right, and ask them to frame the Baroque facade behind you (check the exact spot when you're there).
card.rules_and_safety: Access to the courtyard and museums may vary, so check the official site before you go. Flash is usually not allowed inside the museums.
card.challenge: Get one wide shot of the whole Zwinger, then walk a few steps and find a statue that looks like it's judging your outfit.
card.good_to_know: The Zwinger began in 1709 as an orangery, garden and festival ground for Augustus the Strong. Its name comes from a medieval word for the strip of ground between two defensive walls. Heavy bomb damage in February 1945 was followed by rebuilding in the 1950s and 1960s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 75 m north-west of the Zwinger, at the phone icon on the map, and face south-east. You'll be looking across the whole complex instead of up at one wall.

card.hook: Most people walk onto the Augustusbrücke to look at the river and end up pointing their phone at a whole skyline instead. Dresden Castle sits right in the middle of it, with the Frauenkirche and the Semperoper alongside.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Augustusbrücke, about 350 m north-east of the subject. Face south-west and let the buildings line up in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the bridge, the skyline and the sky in one frame. Then try 1x for a cleaner view, and 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick the castle out of the skyline.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and keep the skyline level, then let the bridge railing or pavement lead the eye toward the castle.
card.best_time: Soft light in the morning or in the hour before sunset is kinder than harsh midday sun. Early in the day also usually means fewer people on the bridge.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Georgentor on the Schlossplatz, use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the palace gate over your shoulder. Another option is Sophienstraße from the Taschenberg end, facing the palace.
card.ask_someone: For a photo of you with the castle and the Hofkirche, try the back corner of the Theaterplatz, near the Zwinger café a short way up the slope, and ask a passer-by to shoot you from there.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the castle, flash and selfie sticks are not allowed, though private photography is generally fine. Parts of the museum need advance booking, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Get the castle, the Frauenkirche and the Semperoper all in one shot, with the bridge railing leading your eye in.
card.good_to_know: Dresden Castle, also called the Royal Palace, was home to the electors and kings of Saxony for almost 400 years. It began as a Romanesque keep around 1200, and the Hausmannsturm tower dates from the early 15th century. The bombing of 13 February 1945 left most of it a roofless shell, and restoration is still going on.

card.hook: Most grand buildings make you squeeze yourself into the frame. The Semperoper gives you a whole square to step back in, so the full front and the panther chariot on top fit in one shot.
card.stand_here: Stand in Theaterplatz, on the west side of the square near the King Johann statue, about 75 m south of the subject. Face north and the opera is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole facade with the King Johann monument in front. Use zoom 0.5x only if the building won't fit, and keep the phone level. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for the chariot and sculptures above the portal.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and line up the facade with them, so the vertical lines stay straight.
card.best_time: Go before the afternoon, when the front of the building gets its light. After dusk is lovely too, because the facade is lit up.
card.selfie_here: In Theaterplatz, stand in front of the King Johann statue in the middle of the square and face away from the opera, using the front camera. For a different backdrop, try the western end of the Brühl's Terrace, where the opera can be in view behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask someone to stand on the Augustusbrücke at the Theaterplatz end, facing the opera, while you stand in front of them between them and the opera (it's worth a quick check that the view still works).
card.rules_and_safety: Theaterplatz is an open public square. If you want to go inside the opera house, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one shot with King Johann low in the frame and the panther chariot near the top, then see if your friends can spot Dionysos.
card.good_to_know: Gottfried Semper's first opera house opened here in 1841. After a fire in 1869, the citizens asked for Semper to rebuild it, but he was in exile, so his son Manfred built the second house to his plans, finished in 1878. The building was largely destroyed in 1945, and the reconstruction was completed on 13 February 1985, very close to its pre-war look.

card.hook: Augustus III was a Catholic ruler in a mostly Protestant city, and he built a cathedral that is impossible to miss. From the river end of the terrace, you can fit the cathedral, the castle and the Elbe into one photo.
card.stand_here: Go to the Brühlsche Terrasse, about 220 m east of the subject, and head for the stairs at the river end. Face west and the cathedral's facade and dome line up with the Residenzschloss, with the Elbe in front.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the facade, dome, castle and river in one shot. Try 0.5x if you want more foreground, or 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for a tighter shot of the dome and tower.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the lit stonework, then drag the slider a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Go at blue hour, just after sunset or just before sunrise, when the stonework stands out against a deep sky. Switch on night mode and rest your elbows on the stairs or railing to keep your phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to Schlossplatz, on the square beside the palace, and stand with the church's facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x to fit the tall front in, and keep the landmark over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by on Theaterplatz to stand where both the church front and the Residenzschloss beside it are visible, then pose in front of them.
card.rules_and_safety: The Brühlsche Terrasse and its stairs may have access changes or closures, so check the official site before you go. If you step inside the cathedral, skip the flash during services.
card.challenge: Turn on the gridlines and get the cathedral on one vertical line and the river along the bottom third, with the castle in the frame too.
card.good_to_know: Gaetano Chiaveri designed the cathedral between 1738 and 1751 for Augustus III. It was badly damaged in February 1945 and restored by 1962. Inside, the crypts of the Wettin family hold the heart of Augustus the Strong.

card.hook: Imagine a stone balcony high over the river, with grand buildings and statues lined up along it like they're queuing for a photo. No wonder people nicknamed Brühl's Terrace "The Balcony of Europe".
card.stand_here: Stand on Brühl's Terrace about 250 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. Then stroll along the terrace for closer shots of the staircase, the statues and the Albertinum.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to get the whole view along the terrace. If the balustrade and buildings won't fit, drop to zoom 0.5x, then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for statues and details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the buildings, then slide it a touch darker if the sky is bright, so the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon gives you softer light and a quieter terrace. Check the weather too, because the open view over the river looks best with some sky.
card.selfie_here: Try the staircase on the west side of the terrace, the one that leads down toward Schlossplatz. Reviewers love the view down these stairs, so use the front camera, hold it a little low, and try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more of the scene. Check on site that the spot feels right.
card.rules_and_safety: Please check locally for current access before you go.
card.challenge: Find a statue or a lamp for your foreground, line the balustrade up on a diagonal with the gridlines, and see if you can keep the horizon dead level.
card.good_to_know: The terrace began as part of the city's fortifications, rebuilt after the Schmalkaldic War of 1546/47. It's named after Count Heinrich von Brühl, who was given the whole terrace in 1747, and it opened to the public in 1814. The area was destroyed in February 1945, but it's been rebuilt and now looks very much as it did in the past.

card.hook: Picture 35 rulers on horseback stretched along 102 metres of wall, in a street so narrow you can't squeeze them all into one photo. Good news: you don't have to, because this is a photo series, not a single shot.
card.stand_here: Start in the Stallhof courtyard: stand about 65 m south-west of the subject, in Stallhof, and face north-east. The white arches and columns make a calm frame around the wall.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x for the arches and columns. Try 0.5x if you want a long stretch of the street in the frame, then zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) for single riders and tile details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the tiles on the map-side of the wall, and if bright sun hits part of it, slide the picture a little darker so the cream tiles keep their detail.
card.best_time: The wall gets direct sun for only a few minutes a day, so bright, overcast light is the easiest. Keep the flash off either way.
card.selfie_here: Head to the far end of the wall by the Hofkirche, on the Augustusstraße/Schlossplatz side. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the mural and the Frauenkirche dome sit behind you, then check the framing when you get there.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the Hofkirche end of the mural while you stand along the wall, so the whole wall fits in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photography is allowed at the Fürstenzug. Please avoid flash and give other visitors room to pass.
card.challenge: Skip the princes for a minute and find the ordinary folk: can you photograph a child, a farmer and a craftsman on the wall?
card.good_to_know: The Fürstenzug was first painted between 1871 and 1876 by Wilhelm Walther to mark 800 years of the House of Wettin. The paint wore badly, so from 1904 to 1907 it was recreated on about 23,000 Meissen porcelain tiles. It shows rulers from 1127 to 1904, each with their name written beneath.

card.hook: Nine sandstone arches march across the Elbe, and every few minutes a tram trundles over them like it's on a model railway. Wait for one, and you've got the shot.
card.stand_here: Stand at the phone icon on the map, about 100 m north-east of the subject, and face south-west towards the Augustus Bridge. From here you can fit the whole span in, not just the roadway.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to fit the arches and the river in. Move closer and try 0.5x if you want the full span. Zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) is great for picking out a single arch or a tram.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on gridlines and line the parapet or the tops of the arches up with a horizontal line, so the bridge sits nice and level.
card.best_time: Early morning or around sunset usually gives softer light and fewer people on the pavements. After dark, use night mode and rest your phone against something solid for a sharper shot.
card.selfie_here: Try Brühl's Terrace, the riverside terrace between the Augustus Bridge and the Carolabrücke, where the bridge can be your backdrop. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and tilt so the bridge sits behind your shoulder (check the angle on site).
card.ask_someone: Head to the Canaletto-Blick on the Neustadt riverbank near the bridge and ask a passer-by to frame you with the bridge and the Old Town skyline.
card.rules_and_safety: It's a working road bridge, so keep clear of the tram tracks and traffic. If you need details of any works or closures, check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Catch a tram halfway across the bridge, with the arches lined up under it, and see if you can do it in three shots or fewer.
card.good_to_know: The current bridge has nine arches and was built between 1907 and 1910 to designs by Wilhelm Kreis and Theodor Klette. It replaced a 12-arch sandstone bridge from 1727 to 1731, built under Augustus II the Strong, which was taken down to give river traffic a wider opening. A stone bridge was first built here in 1220, so it's a very old crossing.

card.hook: Walk past Pfunds Molkerei and you might not even slow down. The front is a plain facade with no hint of the hand-painted tiles inside. That's what makes it a fun first photo in your set.

card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for a natural view of the shop front. If the pavement is too narrow to step back, try zoom 0.5x to fit the whole facade in, or zoom 2x for a closer shot of the sign and shop window.

card.hook: Walk out into the middle of the Altmarkt and there it is: one tall tower and a plain, broad front, standing out against the old-town buildings like it's posing for you. It's the natural postcard spot, so you can't really get it wrong.
card.stand_here: The church sits across the open square with Altstadt buildings framing it on either side.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the tower and the whole front together, and step back if the top gets cut off. Try 0.5x if you want more of the square around you, or 2x-5x (depends on your phone) to pick out details high up the tower.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the tower up against a vertical one, then tap the sky and slide a little darker so it stays blue and the stonework keeps its detail.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, and go earlier in the morning if you want fewer people in the square. In Advent the Striezelmarkt Christmas market fills the Altmarkt and can block this view, so try Pfarrgasse, the narrow lane nearby, to get the church at the end of an old-town street.
card.selfie_here: Head to the Julius Otto memorial beside the church exterior on the Altmarkt, next to the statue of a choirboy in a blue suit. Use the front camera (try 0.5x if yours has it) and keep the church right behind your shoulder, with the choirboy as a friendly prop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand out on the Altmarkt facing the church, so the tower and the whole front fit in the frame, while you pose in front of the church.
card.rules_and_safety: Photo rules inside the church seem to vary, so ask before you take any pictures there. The church is a working place of worship, and the tower climb is separate, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Can you get the tower dead straight on a gridline, with a little sky above it and not a single stranger's head in the way?
card.good_to_know: The Kreuzkirche is the largest church building in Saxony and the home of the Dresdner Kreuzchor boys' choir. It was dedicated to the Holy Cross in 1388, but what you see today is mostly late 1700s work, after Prussian guns wrecked the earlier church in the Seven Years' War. The last fire came during the bombing of Dresden on 13 February 1945, and the church reopened in 1955.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand in the Altmarkt, about 120 m north-west of the subject (that's the phone icon on the map), and face south-east. The church sits across the open square with Altstadt buildings framing it on either side.

card.hook: Picture a little pleasure palace sitting perfectly still on the water, with a twin hanging upside down beneath it. That's the Großer Garten's big moment, and you don't need any photo skills to get it.
card.stand_here: Face west and the palace sits across the water, with trees closing in on both sides.
card.zoom: Start at 1x so the palace and its reflection both fit. If you want a tighter shot of the facade, try 2x or higher (depends on your phone). Use 0.5x only if trees or people force you to stand close.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the palace, then slide the brightness down a little so the facade doesn't wash out and the reflection stays rich.
card.best_time: Aim for the evening, when the palace is lit up and the pond picks up the glow. Take a few shots in case ripples blur the reflection.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x if your phone has it, and hold it a bit low and out to the side. Turn so the big building is over your shoulder, not behind your head.
card.rules_and_safety: The park is big, so wear comfy shoes. If you want to go inside the palace, check the official site first, as the building may have its own visiting arrangements.
card.challenge: Turn on gridlines, keep the phone level, and get the palace and its reflection in one shot without a single wonky wall.
card.good_to_know: The Großer Garten is a Baroque park laid out in 1676 on the orders of John George III, Elector of Saxony. It has been open to the public since 1814. The palace at its centre is a Lustschloss, which means a small pleasure palace.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Palaisteich, the pond in front of the palace, and stand about 110 m east of the subject, right at the phone icon. Face west and the palace sits across the water, with trees closing in on both sides.

card.hook: Picture a big stone dome with rows of tall townhouses crowding in around it, like they all want to be in the photo too. That's Neumarkt, and it's a gift for your phone.
card.stand_here: The dome sits in the centre with the baroque-style houses framing the square on either side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x, which gives you the dome and the houses on both sides. Tap 0.5x if you want the whole dome and more rooftops, or 2x and up (depends on your phone) to pick out the dome or a single facade.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and put the dome on the centre line, then tap the church stonework and slide a little darker if the sky is washing out.
card.best_time: Go early in the morning if you can. The square is empty then, so nobody walks through your shot.
card.selfie_here: Find the Martin Luther statue on Neumarkt, right in front of the Frauenkirche, and stand beside it with the church facade behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the church over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the east side of Neumarkt while you stand with the Frauenkirche behind you, so they can fit the whole church into the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: There's construction work near the square, so look for scaffolding and any closures before you set up. If you want to go inside the church, check the official Frauenkirche site first.
card.challenge: Take one shot with the dome dead centre and the houses perfectly balanced left and right, then see if a friend can spot which one is the 'level' one.
card.good_to_know: Neumarkt became the 'New Market' when the city walls were extended in 1530, as the second market square alongside the Altmarkt. Under August II the Strong it was lined with baroque buildings. The area was almost completely destroyed in the firestorm of February 1945, and the Frauenkirche was finished again in 2005. The houses around it have been rebuilt in stages since then.

The two sources for the passer-by spot point in opposite directions: Homeoftravel recommends photographing from the east side of Neumarkt to capture the whole church, while Explorest describes a photo taken from the Neumarkt centre facing east towards the church (that is, from the west side). Check both on the ground. The Explorest page also gives coordinates of 51°03'06"N, 13°44'25"E, which fall close to the position you supplied. No page mentioned selfie-stick or tripod rules for this square. Several sources are older (the Wikimedia and Heymarty pages are 2 to 8 years old).

card.hook: Augustus the Strong wanted a palace to show off his Japanese porcelain, and the result is one of the most photogenic buildings on Dresden's Neustadt bank. It's big, formal and symmetrical, with greenery out front that works as a ready-made foreground.
card.stand_here: Stand about 170 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From there the Japanese Palace and some of its garden should fill the middle of your frame.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the whole scene. Then go to 2x for a tighter shot of the facade. If you walk closer into the garden, 0.5x helps you fit the whole front in.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines and line the roofline up with a horizontal line, so the walls and roof stay nice and straight.
card.best_time: Morning or late afternoon gives softer light and fewer people in your shot. At bright midday the sky can overpower the building, so tap the palace and slide it a bit darker.
card.selfie_here: Walk round from the front to the Palaisgarten on the Elbe side of the palace, which is a good spot for a palace view. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the palace over your shoulder. Check the screen to make sure the building is in the shot.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the Palaisplatz, the square in front of the palace, and shoot toward the front of the building with you in front of the facade.
card.rules_and_safety: Inside the permanent exhibitions, photos are for private use only, with no flash and no selfie sticks, and you need to keep 50 cm from other people. Check the official site before you go to see which parts of the grounds you can enter.
card.challenge: Get a shot where the garden frames the bottom of the picture and the roofline sits dead straight on a gridline. No wonky palaces allowed.
card.good_to_know: The palace dates from 1715. Between 1729 and 1731 it was extended so Augustus the Strong could display his porcelain, but that plan was never carried out and it later served as the Saxon Library. It was damaged in the bombing raids of 13 February 1945, and the French government restored much of the palace and gardens, finishing in the 1980s. Today it houses three museums.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand about 170 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east. From there the Japanese Palace and some of its garden should fill the middle of your frame.

card.hook: Picture a mosque dome and minarets sitting behind a Dresden railway line. Surprise: it's a cigarette factory dressed up as one, and that's exactly why everyone stops to photograph it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the Brühlsche Terrasse, about 1.1 km south-east of the subject, and face north-west. Head for the Elbe-bank end, looking across the river towards the Neustadt side.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 2x to 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pull the dome and chimney closer. Then switch to zoom 1x for a wider shot with the river and sky. Skip 0.5x here, because the Yenidze would look tiny.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the dome, then drag the slider to make the picture a little darker so the lit dome keeps its colour against the sky.
card.best_time: Go in the evening, in the half hour after sunset, when the dome is lit and the sky still has some colour. Turn on night mode, rest your elbows on the parapet to keep the phone steady, and take several shots, because zoomed-in photos get softer in low light.
card.selfie_here: Try the pavement on Weißeritzstraße in front of the Yenidze (No. 3). Stand on the street side of the building, use the front camera (zoom 0.5x if your phone has it), and let the dome and mosque-style facade fill the frame over your shoulder. If you fancy a higher angle, the top floor of the car park across the street is worth a try, though we haven't confirmed it works for selfies.
card.ask_someone: On the Marienbrücke, hand your phone to a passer-by and ask them to frame you so the dome and the minaret-style chimney rise above the railway behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The Brühlsche Terrasse is an open public promenade, but access near the Carolabrücke end may be affected by the 2024 bridge collapse, so check current access on the day. The Yenidze is an office building with a restaurant, so check the official site before you go if you want to go inside.
card.challenge: Spot the chimney that's pretending to be a minaret, then get it and the dome in one shot, with a bit of sky above.
card.good_to_know: The Yenidze was built between 1907 and 1909 for a tobacco company, designed by Martin Hammitzsch. Its Moorish Revival look was meant to recall the eastern origins of tobacco and to work as advertising, and it was never a mosque. It has about 600 windows and a dome 20 metres high, and was restored in 1996. It's now used as offices.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the Brühlsche Terrasse (the phone icon on the map), about 1.1 km south-east of the subject, and face north-west. Head for the Elbe-bank end, looking across the river towards the Neustadt side.

card.hook: Cyclists glide past behind you, the Elbe slides by in front, and the far bank looks like it's posing for you. This is the Canaletto-Blick, and it's a lovely spot to just stop and look.
card.stand_here: At the Canaletto-Blick on the Elberadweg, stand about 140 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.
card.zoom: Start at 1x to get the whole scene, with the river along the bottom and the far bank across the middle. Try 0.5x for more sky and path in front of you, then 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out single buildings.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on the lower third line, and keep the phone level so the buildings don't lean.
card.best_time: Late afternoon to early evening is usually the most flattering for a riverside view like this. Pick a clear day and check where the sun is before you set up.
card.selfie_here: Look for the red picture frame on the Elberadweg, a short way west of the Augustusbrücke, in front of the Hotel Bellevue grounds. Use the front camera (0.5x if your phone has it) and turn so the skyline is over your shoulder. The frame's status has been reported differently, so check when you arrive. The view works even without it.
card.rules_and_safety: Walkers and cyclists use this path, so wait for a clear gap and keep your elbows in. It's a public area, but check the official site before you go in case of closures or works on the path.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot with the river in the foreground and one tighter shot of a single building, then see which one you'd actually frame.
card.good_to_know: The spot is called Canaletto-Blick (Canaletto view) and sits on the Elberadweg in Dresden's Innere Neustadt. The path runs right along the water, so a few steps either way give you new angles. Looking through the red frame shows the same skyline Canaletto painted in 1748.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: At the Canaletto-Blick on the Elberadweg, stand about 140 m south-west of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face north-east.

selfie_spots.why: Standing at the Neustädter Elbufer below Hotel Bellevue and looking through the red frame gives the same skyline Canaletto painted in 1748.

card.hook: Tall funnels, chunky paddle boxes and a wide stretch of river out front: the Elbe steamers look like they know you're about to take a picture.
card.stand_here: Head to the Terrassenufer on the Elbe in Dresden's Altstadt and stand about 260 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face west, and the paddle steamers sit at the far end of the view.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x to catch the whole riverside, with water in front and city behind. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to pull in a funnel or paddle wheel, and hold the phone with both hands. Use 0.5x only if you walk right up to a boat.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the river along the lower third, park the boat on a side line and leave a good bit of sky above.
card.best_time: Morning is a good bet, since the sun is behind you as you look west and tends to light the boats more evenly. Evening can bring warm colour to the sky, but the boats may look darker against it.
card.selfie_here: Try the railing on the Brühlsche Terrasse, the terrace above the Terrassenufer, where you look out over the piers where the steamers are moored. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the view over your shoulder, but check the framing on the spot, as we couldn't confirm the steamers sit directly behind you.
card.ask_someone: Try the Augustusbrücke, where you look down on the steamers at the pier with Brühl's Terrace and the Frauenkirche behind, and hand your phone to a passer-by (the pier layout may have changed, so check the view first).
card.rules_and_safety: The 1 May fleet parade (Flottenparade) may affect when the steamers are at the pier.
card.challenge: Get one funnel on a gridline, then crouch by the water's edge and see if you can catch a boat in its reflection.
card.good_to_know: The paddle steamers at the Terrassenufer are one of Dresden's classic Elbe scenes. The Terrassenufer runs along the river in the Altstadt, in the Seevorstadt area on the edge of the old town centre. Which boats are there, and where they sit, can change from day to day, so build your picture around whatever you find.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the Terrassenufer on the Elbe in Dresden's Altstadt and stand about 260 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map. Face west, and the paddle steamers sit at the far end of the view.
